title: Pandemic surveillance and mobilities across Sydney, New South Wales
thesis: The paper argues that COVID-19 surveillance in Sydney deepened uneven sensory power, leaving lasting scars in Western Sydney despite dismantling of overt tools.
theme_1_justification: Tangential mention of 'function creep' (Vitak & Zimmer, 2020) noting repurposing of technologies, but no explicit dual-use discussion or technology transfer between civilian and military domains.
theme_2_justification: References privacy concerns and Kitchin's call to document new surveillance regime, but does not substantively engage with algorithmic opacity or epistemic authority of data systems.
theme_3_justification: Substantive engagement with sensory power (Isin & Ruppert, 2020) and continuous modulation of mobilities through apps, QR codes, and location tracking; the city is treated as a space of governance through live surveillance.
theme_4_justification: Discusses uneven enforcement and spatial restrictions in Western Sydney but does not address spatial destruction, domicide, or weaponisation of civilian infrastructure.
key_quotes: We argue that these technologies are examples of sensory power which rapidly enrolled human bodies in systems of surveillance that were difficult to unravel through 2022 and beyond.
the idea of 'back to normal' is troubled by the experiences of lockdowns and policing of mobilities in different parts of Sydney.

as the response to the crisis unfolds there is a need for geographers and others to document the ways in which a new surveillance and biopolitical regime is being produced through the alliance of government control and surveillance capitalism and their use of a range of technologies.
policy_relevance: None explicit, but highlights the need for equitable crisis response and awareness of lasting community impacts.
